name: Diamond Sutra of Dunhuang
what: A five-metre scroll of the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, printed from woodblocks and dated the 15th day of the 4th month of the 9th year of Xiantong: 11 May 868. It is the oldest dated printed book known.
why: A book printed six centuries before Gutenberg, sealed in a cave for nine centuries, and sold to a British explorer by a Daoist caretaker who needed money to restore his temple.
now: British Library, London (Or.8210/P.2). Digitised by the International Dunhuang Project.
dispute: Many in China regard Stein's purchases at Dunhuang as theft.

sources.cite: Wood, F. & Barnard, M. (2010). The Diamond Sutra: The Story of the World's Earliest Dated Printed Book. British Library.
Hansen, V. (2012). The Silk Road: A New History. Oxford University Press.

stops.note: The colophon says Wang Jie had it made "for universal free distribution, on behalf of his two parents". The date is sure; where it was printed is not, perhaps Dunhuang itself, perhaps Chang'an or Sichuan.
stops.meet: a monk copying sutras at the Mogao caves

stops.note: Around the year 1000 tens of thousands of manuscripts were walled up in a side chamber of Cave 16. Why is still argued: fear of invaders, or a store for worn-out scriptures.
In June 1900 the self-appointed Daoist guardian of the caves, Wang Yuanlu, found the walled-up door while clearing sand.
The Hungarian-British explorer Aurel Stein bought the scroll with thousands of manuscripts for a small donation to Wang's restoration fund. Paul Pelliot took more the next year.
The crates went west by camel and ship and reached London around 1909.
The British Library, split from the Museum in 1973, moved to its new building at St Pancras in 1997.
